abstract: We introduce a new Bayesian perspective on the concept of data reconstruction, and leverage this viewpoint to propose a new security definition that, in certain settings, provably prevents reconstruction attacks. We use our paradigm to shed new light on one of the most notorious attacks in the privacy and memorization literature - fingerprinting code attacks (FPC). We argue that these attacks are really a form of membership inference attacks, rather than reconstruction attacks. Furthermore, we show that if the goal is solely to prevent reconstruction (but not membership inference), then in some cases the impossibility results derived from FPC no longer apply.

      Abstract
We introduce a new Bayesian perspective on the concept of data reconstruction, and leverage
this viewpoint to propose a new security definition that, in certain settings, provably prevents
reconstruction attacks. We use our paradigm to shed new light on one of the most notorious attacks
in the privacy and memorization literature – fingerprinting code attacks (FPC). We argue that
these attacks are really a form of membership inference attacks, rather than reconstruction attacks.
Furthermore, we show that if the goal is solely to prevent reconstruction (but not membership
inference), then in some cases the impossibility results derived from FPC no longer apply.

 1      Introduction
Carlini et al. [10] showed that it is sometimes possible to extract unique pieces of training data
from modern language models (such as credit card numbers). This demonstrates that such
models can unintentionally memorize rare parts of their training data, even if those parts
appear only once. Since then, this memorization phenomenon has been studied in a long
line of work, providing increasingly many examples in which modern models unintentionally
memorize data. In fact, several follow-up papers have shown that there exist learning tasks
for which memorization is provably necessary [17, 18, 11, 3, 19, 7, 8, 9].

           However, these prior works did not converge on a single definition of memorization, and
       instead considered several context-dependent notions. Loosely speaking, existing definitions
       can be grouped into two main types:
           Extractable memorization. Some papers, such as Carlini et al. [10], define memor-
           ization in terms of extraction. Informally, a model h is said to “memorize” a training
           example x if x can be extracted from h. This is in line with the cryptographic concept of
           knowledge extraction in proofs of knowledge: To demonstrate that Alice “knows” a fact
           there should be a way to extract that fact from her.
           Informational memorization. Other works, such as Brown et al. [3], define memoriza-
           tion using statistical or information-theoretic criteria. For example, a model h is said to
           “memorize” a training example x if the mutual information between h and x is high. This
           is in line with the information-theoretic view of knowledge: A system is considered to
           possess information about a variable if observing the system reduces uncertainty about
           that variable.
           In light of this, our work is motivated by the following questions:

           Is there a difference between extractable memorization and informational memorization?
             Could a model be considered “memorizing” under one definition but not the other?

           We provide positive answers to the above questions. Specifically, we show that there are
       well-established examples of informational memorization in which “extraction” is provably
       impossible. This raises the question of whether “informational memorization” should be
       considered as a form of “memorization” at all. After all, if it is impossible for an attacker to
       extract information from the model, then has the model really memorized it? (And even if it
       has, do we care about it?) In more detail, our contributions are as follows.
       1. We propose a new security definition, computational in nature, such that algorithms that
          satisfy it are guaranteed to resist extraction attacks. Our definition is deliberately as
          permissive as possible while still preventing extraction attacks. Unlike other security
          notions, such as differential privacy [15], we do not aim to rule out all possible privacy
          breaches. Indeed, while differential privacy prevents extraction attacks, it also provably
          prevents “informational memorization” as studied in prior work. Thus, differential privacy
          cannot be leveraged to separate informational from extractable memorization.
       2. We revisit the celebrated marginals problem, which is one of the most notoriously hard
          problems in the literature on differential privacy. In this problem, our input is an n×d
          matrix A and the goal is to approximate the average of the rows of A. The seminal work
          of Bun, Ullman, and Vadhan [6] showed that the marginals  √     problem is unsolvable with
          differential privacy (with non-trivial utility) unless n > d. Their hard instance is based
          on the concept of fingerprinting codes (FPC)1 , and specifically, the FPC construction
          given by Tardos [34]. Since then, Tardos’ FPC has been used to show many negative
          results in various settings2 . We show that Tardos’ hard instance for the marginals problem
          can in fact be solved while
                                    √ satisfying our new security notion, thereby resisting extraction
          attacks even when n ≪ d. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to show
          that formal security√ notions of any kind can be achieved for Tardos’ hard instance when
          n is smaller than d.

3. Attias et al. [1] presented a Stochastic Convex Optimization (SCO) problem such that
   any algorithm for solving it must provably exhibit large memorization (according to their
   notion of informational memorization, to be surveyed in Section 1.1). The hard instance
   underlying their construction is precisely Tardos’ FPC, for which we present a secure
   mechanism (under our new security definition). Thus, while the SCO problem studied by
   Attias et al. [1] necessitates informational memorization, we show that (under the same
   conditions) it can in fact be solved while resisting extraction attacks, thereby separating
   informational from extractable memorization.

1.1      Existing definitions of informational memorization
To motivate our new security definition, we now survey some of the existing definitions of
informational memorization. We will then present examples of mechanisms that exhibit large
memorization according to these informational definitions, while at the same time resisting
extraction. One such definition, proposed by Brown et al. [3], casts memorization in terms of
conditional mutual information as follows.

▶ Definition 1 ([3]). Let Prior be a meta-distribution (i.e., a distribution over distributions).
Let Nature be a target distribution sampled from Prior, and let S be a sample from Nature.
Let h ← M(S) be a model obtained by running a learning algorithm M on the sample S.
The amount of information that h memorizes about S is defined as I(S; h| Nature).

    In this definition, the meta-distribution Prior is assumed to be known, but the specific
target distribution Nature is a priori unknown. To interpret this definition, consider a learning
algorithm M that given a sample S attempts to learn properties of the underlying distribution
Nature, for instance, to identify a good predictor h. Now note that I(S; h| Nature) captures
the amount of information that h encodes about S after excluding information about the
target distribution itself. Intuitively, this means that I(S; h| Nature) captures the amount of
information encoded in h that is “unique to the dataset”.
   Attias et al. [1] considered a different definition for memorization, stated in terms of
membership inference attacks (MIA) [30, 37]. Membership inference is a type of attack in
which, given a model h and a data point x, the attacker aims to determine whether x was
part of the training data underlying the model h. Formally,

▶ Definition 2 ([30, 37, 1, 36]). Let X be a data domain. Let M be an algorithm whose input
is a dataset containing n elements from X . Algorithm M is (m ∈ N, ξ ∈ (0, 1))-memorizing
if there is a distribution D over X and a distinguisher A such that

        Pr      [b = “In”] ≥         and         Pr      [b = “In”] ≤ ξ
      S←D n                    n               S←D n
     h←M(S)                                   h←M(S)

    In words, the attacker A is executed on h ← M(S) and on a data point x ∈ X . If this x
is sampled uniformly3 from S, then there is a noticeable probability (at least m/n) that A
correctly determines that x ∈ S. This is intended to capture the intuition that h “memorizes”
m out of the n elements of S. On the other hand, when x is instead sampled from the
underlying distribution D, the probability that A falsely determines that x ∈ S should be
small (at most ξ).

       1.2    Warmup: Memorization can be ambiguous
       We continue our motivating discussion by surveying the following example whose memorization
       behavior is “formally ambiguous”.

       ▶ Example 3. Let n, d ∈ N be parameters where d is even, let Nature be the uniform
       distribution over {0, 1}d , and let S = (x1 , . . . , xn ) ← Naturen be a sample containing n iid
       elements from Nature. We think of S as an n × d binary matrix. Consider the mechanism
       M that, given S, returns an n × d2 matrix H where H[i, j] = S[i, 2j − 1] ⊕ S[i, 2j].

           In this example, we have that I(S; H| Nature) = nd/2 (intuitively, this holds because
       given H the number of choices for every pair of bits in S drops from 4 to 2). So M memorizes
       a lot of information about S according to Definition 1. In addition, there is a trivial
       membership inference attack against this mechanism. Specifically, given the release H and a
       row x ∈ {0, 1}d , the attacker answers “In” if and only if x is consistent with a row in H; i.e.,
       there is a row i ∈ [n] such that for every coordinate j ∈ [d/2] we have H[i, j] = x2j−1 ⊕ x2j .
       Note that for every x ∈ S we have that A(H, x) = “In”. But for a random x ∈ {0, 1}d we
       have that Pr[A(H, x) = “In”] ≤ n · 2−d/2 . So M essentially “memorizes” all elements in S
       according to Definition 2; formally it is (n, n·2−d/2 )-memorizing.
           However, even given the release H, the marginal distribution on any single bit in S is still
       completely uniform. Furthermore, even given H, no attacker (even unbounded) can guess
       noticeably more than half of the coordinates of any single row in S. Therefore, while there
       is a strong sense in which M “memorizes” a lot of information (according to Definitions 1
       and 2), there is also a strong sense in which no attacker can extract training examples from
       H. It is therefore open to interpretation whether this should be considered memorization
       or not.

       1.3    Our security definition: arguing about the attacker’s knowledge is
              crucial
       Example 3 is simple enough so that we could argue that “extraction is impossible” without
       formally defining what it means. This becomes much less clear when dealing with more
       involved algorithms/problems. In order to tackle this, we will introduce a formal security
       definition that prevents extraction and then present algorithms satisfying our definition.
       Building up towards our security definition, we now argue that such a definition must take
       into account the attacker’s side-information (or lack thereof) about the sample and/or the
       underlying distribution.

       ▶ Example 4. Consider again Example 3, where the mechanism M takes a dataset S
       containing nd random bits and releases nd 2 “parity bits” (denoted as H). As we mentioned, in
       this scenario no attacker can guess noticeably more than half of the bits of any single row in S.
       However, this argument clearly breaks down if the attacker possesses enough side-information
       about the sample S. For example, suppose that the attacker knows a superset S of size n10
       that contains S as well as additional (n10 − n) independent samples from {0, 1}d . Now, if the
       attacker knows S and sees the release H, then it can easily identify all rows in S with high
       confidence. Specifically, the attacker searches for all rows in S that are consistent with a row
       in H. This identifies all rows in S, and the probability of falsely identifying a row outside of
       S is bounded by 2−d/2 · poly(n).

           But did the attacker really extract S from the release H, or was it already encoded in the
       side-information available to it? Taking this example to the limit, suppose that the attacker’s
       side-information explicitly specifies a vector x∗ from the sample S. Here it is intuitively clear
H. Kaplan, Y. Mansour, K. Nissim, and U. Stemmer                                                   84:5


that if this attacker sees the release H and then “identifies” that x∗ ∈ S, then this is not a
very successful attack, as this information was not derived from the release H in any way.
An alternative way to interpret this is that we cannot hope to defend against “extracting”
x∗ by attackers who already “know” that x∗ ∈ S. What about attackers who know that
there is a 99% chance that x∗ ∈ S? What about 10%? This suggests that we need some
way of quantifying the amount of side-information the attacker possessed about the element
that it chooses to reconstruct before seeing the release. Furthermore, we argue that there are
cases where limiting the amount of side-information the attacker has about S is insufficient,
and we must also consider the amount of side-information it has about the underlying data
distribution.

▶ Example 5. Let us consider the following variant of Example 4. Suppose that the data
distribution Nature is generated at random, by first randomly sampling a set S ⊆ {0, 1}d
of size n10 , and then defining Nature to be uniform over S. Now a sample S of size n is
sampled from Nature and we compute H ← M(S), where M is the same mechanism from
the previous two examples. As in Example 4, an attacker that knows S and sees the release
H can easily reconstruct all of S. But now the side information that the attacker possesses
is more about the underlying distribution Nature rather than about the sample S, in the
sense that conditioned on Nature the attacker does not hold any side-information.

    This is actually reminiscent of the way some of the negative results are stated in the
literature, e.g., by Attias et al. [1]: The attacker possesses a lot of side information; not
directly on the sample S, but rather through knowledge on the underlying distribution
Nature. Motivated by this, we advocate that in order for a “reconstruction attack” to be
successful, the attacker needs to reconstruct an element z about which it had “little” or
“bounded” knowledge before seeing the release.
    In particular, this means that we need a way to argue about lack of knowledge in order
to be able to designate an attack as successful. We model this via a Bayesian perspective:
We assume that the underlying data distribution Nature is itself a random element, sampled
from a family of possible data distributions Prior. The dataset S is then sampled from
Nature. A data analysis mechanism M is then executed on S and outputs a release H. An
attacker A who knows the meta-distribution Prior (but not Nature and S directly) then sees
the release H and tries to extract information about S from H. We will denote the output
of A as z. Treating both Nature and S as random elements allows us to model the “lack of
knowledge” that the attacker has about them. We will say that the attacker is successful
only if it does not have a lot of prior knowledge, through Nature and S, about z.


Ruling out trivial attacks. Suppose for now that the attacker aims to identify an element
z such that z ∈ S (we will later consider more general types of attacks). Consider the
mechanism Mbot that takes a dataset S, ignores it, and returns ⊥. Clearly, this mechanism
should be considered secure. However, as we assume that the attacker knows Prior, it could
be aware of “trivial” elements which appear in the sample S w.h.p. even over sampling
Nature from Prior. Then, paradoxically, the attacker can “extract” these trivial elements
from the empty release ⊥.

▶ Example 6. Suppose that the meta-distribution Prior is defined via the following process
for sampling Nature. Sample a set S ⊆ {0, 1}d of size n10 and return the distribution Nature
that with probability 0.5 returns ⃗0 and with probability 0.5 returns a uniform element from
S. As the attacker knows Prior, it could simply guess that ⃗0 ∈ S.

           Motivated by this discussion, in Section 3 we present our security definition, called
       Bayesian Extraction-Safe, that prevents an attacker from extracting an element z from the
       training set unless: (1) The attacker possessed “too much” side-information about z before
       seeing the release, as in Examples 4 and 5; or (2) This z is a “trivial” element in the sense
       that it is known a priori (from knowing Prior, even without additional side-information) that
       such an element is likely to appear in the sample, as in Example 6.
           We leverage our new security definition to examine Tardos’ hard instance for the marginals
       problem under different assumptions on the attacker. First, we show that when the attacker
       possesses no side-information, computing the exact average is secure. We then show that
       this is no longer the case when side-information is present, as the exact average allows an
       informed attacker to reconstruct elements about which it had little or no prior knowledge.
       Finally, we show that an alternative (noisy) mechanism remains secure even against an
       attacker with arbitrary side-information, as it still prevents the reconstruction of elements
       about which the attacker has limited prior knowledge.
           We stress that our proposed definition does not provide informational privacy at the level
       provided by differential privacy. Rather, it protects against a family of privacy breaches
       where a large portion of the dataset or of a row in the dataset are extractable from a data
       release (this will be made formal in the actual definition).


        2     Preliminaries
       Our security definition builds on a prior security definition by Cohen et al. [12], called
       Narcissus resiliency. Like our definition, Narcissus resiliency does not rule out attackers that
       reconstruct “trivial” elements. However, our definition is deliberately weaker (less secure) in
       the sense that we also do not rule out the extraction of elements about which the attacker
       possessed “too much” side-information, even if these elements are otherwise “non-trivial”.
       This is crucial to allow us to separate informational from extractable memorization. Indeed,
       Narcissus resiliency is subject to the same limitations as differential privacy in this context:
       it provably rules out both informational and extractable memorization. See Remark 8 below.
           The definition of Narcissus resiliency introduces a relation R, where R(S, z) = 1 if and
       only if z is a “valid reconstruction” of S (or of some data point in S). A simple example to
       keep in mind is R(S, z) ≜ 1{z∈S} . To motivate the definition of Narcissus resiliency, consider
       the relation R(S, z) ≜ 1{z∈S} and consider a distribution over images, such that every large
       enough dataset sampled from this distribution contains the Mona Lisa. In this case, if an
       attacker “reconstructs” the Mona Lisa from the outcome of our mechanism, then this is not
       a very meaningful attack, as this could also be done without accessing the outcome of our
       mechanism (the Mona Lisa is “trivial” in this case). The challenge is to distinguish between
       reconstructing something “specific” to the particular dataset versus reconstructing something
       generic. The key idea in the definition of Narcissus resiliency is its self-referential nature.
       Instead of trying to formally capture what is generic and what is not (which is very nuanced),
       the following definition places this decision on the attacker itself. Intuitively, the definition
       requires the attacker to come up with a valid reconstruction w.r.t. the actual dataset S which
       would not be considered a valid reconstruction w.r.t. a fresh dataset T . The formal definition
       follows.

       ▶ Definition 7 ([12]). Let X be a data domain, let D be a distribution over datasets containing
       elements from X , and let R : X ∗ ×{0, 1}∗ →{0, 1}. Algorithm M is (ε, δ, D, R)-Narcissus-
       resilient if for all attackers A it holds that Pr [R(S, z) = 1] ≤ eε · Pr [R(T, z) = 1]+δ.

 3      A Bayesian analogue for Narcissus resiliency
As we mentioned in the introduction, in this work we advocate that in order to classify
an attack as a “successful reconstruction” we must take into consideration the amount of
side-information the attacker has (or lack thereof). Otherwise, it is unclear whether the
attacker really extracted this reconstruction from the released model/statistics rather than
from its side-information. This is not captured by Definition 7. Thus, our starting point is
to reformulate Definition 7 using a Bayesian perspective, aiming to model the uncertainty
the attacker has about the underlying data distribution.
▶ Definition 9. Let X be a data domain and let Prior be a meta-distribution. That is,
Prior is a distribution over distributions over datasets containing elements from X . Let
R : X ∗ × {0, 1}∗ → {0, 1} be a reconstruction relation. Algorithm M is (ε, δ, Prior, R)-
Bayesian extraction-safe if for all attackers A it holds that

         Pr         [R(S, z) = 1] ≤ eε ·       Pr         [R(T, z) = 1] + δ.                (1)
     Nature←Prior                          Nature←Prior
      S←Nature                              S←Nature
       y←M(S)                               T ←Nature
       z←A(y)                                y←M(S)
                                             z←A(y)

    The interpretation is as follows. Look at the left hand side of Equation (1). First Nature
is drawn. This is a distribution over datasets drawn from the meta-distribution Prior. Then
we draw a dataset S from Nature. The algorithm M trains a model y on the dataset S, and
finally the attacker A uses y to reconstruct an element from S. The predicate R determines
if this reconstruction was successful or not. We say that M is Bayesian extraction-safe if
the probability of a successful reconstruction from S is not much larger than the probability
of reconstructing an element from a fresh sample from Nature which we call T on the right
hand side of Equation (1).
    In this section, we construct an algorithm for the marginals problem (defined below) that
is secure in the sense of Definition 9 under interesting choices of the meta-distribution Prior.
▶ Definition 10. Let n, d ∈ N be parameters. Let M be an algorithm whose input is an n × d
binary matrix. Algorithm M solves the (n, d)-marginals problem with error parameters (α, β)
if for every input matrix S, with probability at least 1 − β, the algorithm returns a vector
y ∈ [0, 1]d satisfying ∥y − Average(S)∥∞ ≤ α, where Average(S) ∈ [0, 1]d is the average of
the rows of S.
    We show that the marginals problem can be securely solved (in the sense of Definition 9)
under the following meta-distribution, which we refer to as the Tardos-Prior. This specific
prior distribution is notoriously hard in the privacy and memorization literature, underlying
many of the existing impossibility results.

       ▶ Definition 11 (Tardos-Prior). Let N ≥ n ∈ N and d ∈ N be parameters. We write
       Tardos(N, d, n) to denote the meta-distribution defined by the following process. To sample a
       distribution form Tardos(N, d, n) do:
       1. Sample parameters p1 , . . . , pd ∈ [0, 1] uniformly and independently.
       2. Generate an N ×d ∈ {0, 1}N ×d matrix C where each entry C[i, j] is sampled independently
           from Ber(pj ).
       3. Return the uniform distribution over S ⊆ C of size n. That is, the distribution of sampling
           n rows from C without repetitions.

       ▶ Remark 12. The FPC construction from Tardos’ seminal paper [34] uses a non-uniform
       distribution on the marginals p1 , . . . , pd . This was later generalized by Dwork et al. [16],
       who showed that any sufficiently smooth and spread out distribution on [0, 1], including the
       uniform distribution, suffices for tracing attacks. The arguments in our paper are not overly
       specific to the particular distribution on the marginals, and so we chose to use the uniform
       distribution for simplicity.
           We next show that the mechanism that returns the exact average is secure for Tardos-Prior.
       Note that we cannot hope to show this for every relation R. In particular the exact average
       is not secure w.r.t. the relation R defined as R(S, z) = 1 iff z is the exact average of S. We
       show that it is secure for natural choices for the relation R.

4.2       An alternative treatment for the attacker’s side-information
So the exact average is not secure w.r.t. Tardos-Prior when the attacker possesses enough
side information. How about a noisy average? Consider the mechanism M that takes a
dataset S ∈ ({0, 1}d )n and returns y = Average(S) + noise. That is, M adds independent
noise to each of the coordinates of the empirical average of S. Now consider an attacker
with the following side-information: A pair of vectors (k1 , k2 ) ∈ ({0, 1}d )2 such that one of
them is a random element from S and the other is a random element from Nature, but we
do not know which is which. Nevertheless, given the release y = Average(S) + noise the
attacker can identify w.h.p. who among k1 , k2 belongs to S, and return it as its reconstructed
element.6 On the other hand, in the “baseline experiment”, given this side information, each
of k1 , k2 is exactly equally likely to be in T . Thus, the attacker would fail to correctly guess
an element of T with probability ≳ 1/2.7
    So the noisy average is not secure w.r.t. Tardos-Prior when the attacker possesses enough
side information. However, one could argue that the attack in this example should not
be considered successful, because the result of the attack (the reconstructed element) was
entirely encoded in the attacker’s side-information. In some sense, the attacker extracted z
more from its side-information than from the release y.
    This discussion suggests that a different treatment for the attacker’s side-information
might be needed. More specifically, we want a way to measure the amount of information that
K contains on z, and require that this quantity is “not too high” in order for the attack to be
considered successful. One could try to quantify this is via standard tools from information
theory, such as the mutual information between K and z, or the conditional entropy of z
given K. Recall, however, that these are both average notions, that do not necessarily have
meaningful implications on the specific instantiations of K and z. That is, it could be that
the mutual information between K and z (as random variables) is very low, but the specific
instantiation of K actually tells us quite a bit about z.
    Motivated by this discussion, we use a “point wise” variant of entropy (and conditional
entropy), known as information content, self-information, or surprisal.

           Lemma 28 can be interpreted in two ways:

        1. If the privacy parameters ε, δ are small then M resists reconstruction attacks in the
           “Narcissus sense” (see Definition 7): The attacker cannot reconstruct anything about S
           that it could not have reconstructed with roughly the same probability about a fresh
           dataset T .

        2. Even if ε is large, provided there is “enough randomness” in the dataset such that the
           probability of reconstruction with respect to a fresh dataset is very small compared to
           e−ε , then M still resists reconstruction attacks as the RHS of Inequality (5) will be small.
           Importantly, our formulation of Bayesian extraction-safety takes into account the lack of
           knowledge or uncertainty that the attacker has about the target distribution Nature, in
           the sense that “enough randomness” is also taken over the sampling of Nature from Prior.
           Note that once Nature is fixed, it could be there is actually not enough randomness in
